title: Looking back: year four
hookLine: the schools, each in its own words
tomorrow: why does a sutta open with 'thus have I heard'?

cards: Every flight safety talk says it: put on your own mask first, then help the person next to you. Some people hear that as selfish. Others hear it as the only way anyone gets helped.
Buddhists have their own long version of that argument, and year four heard it from both sides. Free yourself first, or vow to stay until everyone is free?
Two ideals, the arahant and the bodhisattva, and each school says it in its own words.

teach.b: First voice, the Theravada, the school of the elders. Its ideal is the arahant, one who has finished the journey, free of grief and every fetter, as the Dhammapada puts it.

teach.h: NO ONE SUNK IN MUD PULLS ANOTHER OUT.
teach.b: Its best case comes from a sutta: someone sunk in the mud can't pull another out. Someone who isn't sunk can. Get free, and your help becomes real.
And the arahants in the suttas don't vanish; the Buddha sends his first ones out to wander for the welfare of the many.
Second voice, the Mahayana, the great vehicle, the school of Mai's family's chùa.
Its ideal is the bodhisattva, who vows to awaken for the sake of all beings. The Diamond Sutra has the vow: however many beings there are, I will lead them all to nirvana.
Shantideva, a teacher in that tradition, asks to remain as long as space remains and beings suffer, to ease their pain. Its best case: a freedom that leaves anyone behind isn't finished yet.
Both voices are about compassion. They differ on the shape of the road.
And each keeps a place for the other's ideal: Mahayana temples honor the arahants, and the Theravada tells the Buddha's own past lives, in the Jataka stories, as a bodhisatta on the long road.
Year four didn't pick a winner.
It opened many doors, and walked through each.

how: Theravada Buddhism is practiced in places such as Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos; Mahayana in places such as Vietnam, China, Korea and Japan; many temples of both welcome people from the other.

games.q: your study partner says the bodhisattva ideal is the bigger-hearted one. state the Theravada side's best case in one sentence.
o: you can't pull someone out of the mud while sunk in it; get free, then your help is real.
helping others is a distraction; the path is only about your own escape.
the bodhisattva is a late invention, so that ideal doesn't count at all.
games.why: that's the sutta's own image, and its arahants go out to teach. both schools are about compassion; they differ on the shape of the road.

practice: Bring your palms together at your chest, the gesture called anjali, used in temples of every school you met this year.
Hold it, and on each breath out, silently name one gift a school gave you: a way of sitting, a chant, a story, a question. If one gift keeps coming back, stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Looking back, at year four: the schools, each in its own words, two ideals of one compassion.

orig.note: Pali: one bound for awakening; Sanskrit bodhisattva.

carryVoice: Keep this one: many doors, one teacher behind them. Day four of the summit, done.
